\chapter{Which Way, And What Is Around You}
\label{ch:el-norte-y-el-sur}
\hlchaptermodality{347}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name el norte, el sur, el oeste, el centro and alrededor, and say why three of the four compass points came into Spanish from Germanic sailors rather than from Rome.}

Complete ES-C347-alrededor: send somebody north, south or west, name the middle of a town, and say what encircles it.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el norte]{el norte — north, an English word living in Spanish}

\label{lesson:ES-C347-norte}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{office}, then \emph{station}. (\emph{La oficina}; \emph{la estación}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item ¿dónde está? — the question this answers.
  \item el país — the thing this often divides.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{NOR-te}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{r} is a single tap against the ridge behind your teeth. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el norte} — \textquotedblleft{}the north.\textquotedblright{}

Almost every word you have met so far came down from Latin. This one did not.

Latin's word for the north was \textbf{septentriō}, \emph{the seven plough-oxen} — the seven stars of the Great Bear, wheeling around the pole. It is a beautiful word and Spanish barely uses it.

What Spanish uses instead is Germanic. \textbf{Northa} was the north in the mouths of the sailors who worked the Atlantic and the North Sea, and their four direction words travelled with their trade: into Old French as \textbf{nord}, and from there into Spanish as \textbf{norte}.

So \emph{norte} and English \textbf{north} are not cousins that drifted apart. They are the same word, and the \emph{-e} on the end is the only thing Spanish added to make it pronounceable.

Names remember it. \textbf{Norway} is the \emph{north way}; a \textbf{Norman} was a \emph{north-man}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of the four points, and a reminder that Spanish borrows.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el norte}
  \item \emph{el norte del país}
  \item \emph{la estación está al norte}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \emph{norte} Latin or Germanic? (Germanic.) And what did Latin's own \emph{septentriō} name? (The seven plough-oxen, the stars of the Great Bear.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el sur]{el sur — south, the sunward quarter}

\label{lesson:ES-C347-sur}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{station}, then \emph{north}. (\emph{La estación}; \emph{el norte}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el país — what a direction cuts in half.
  \item la ciudad — what sits in one half or the other.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{SUR}, one beat, and the \emph{r} at the end is a single tap rather than a roll. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el sur} — \textquotedblleft{}the south.\textquotedblright{}

Like \emph{norte}, this came in with Atlantic sailors rather than down from Rome. Germanic \textbf{sunthaz} became Old French \textbf{sud}, and Spanish took it as \textbf{sur}. It is the same word as English \textbf{south}.

What is inside it is a guess, but a good one: \textbf{sun}. Stand anywhere in northern Europe and the sun is never overhead — it swings across the southern half of the sky, all day, all year. The sunward quarter is the south, and so the sun gave its name to a direction.

Spanish has both shapes. \textbf{Sur} on its own, and \textbf{sud-} when it joins onto another word, as in \emph{Sudamérica}.

English does the same trick and never notices: \textbf{south}, but \textbf{southern} with a different vowel, and \textbf{Sussex} for the \emph{South Saxons}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two of the four points, and both of them Germanic.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el sur}
  \item \emph{el norte y el sur}
  \item \emph{la ciudad está al sur}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which everyday thing is probably hiding inside \emph{sur}? (The sun.) And which shape does Spanish use when the word joins onto another? (\emph{Sud-}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el oeste]{el oeste — west, named after the evening}

\label{lesson:ES-C347-oeste}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{north}, then \emph{south}. (\emph{El norte}; \emph{el sur}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item este — a word that will trip you here.
  \item ¿dónde está? — the question all four points answer.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{o-ES-te}, three beats with the weight on the second. The \emph{o} and the \emph{e} stay separate, each with its own beat. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el oeste} — \textquotedblleft{}the west.\textquotedblright{}

The third Germanic borrowing in a row: \textbf{westaz} to Old French \textbf{ouest} to Spanish \textbf{oeste}. Again the same word as English \textbf{west}.

Under it lies an old root meaning \emph{evening}. Latin took that root as \textbf{vesper}, the evening star and then the evening itself, which is why the evening prayers of a monastery are called \textbf{vespers}. So the west is not named for a place. It is named for an hour — the quarter of the sky the sun falls into at the end of the day.

Now the trap. The fourth point, the east, is \textbf{el este} — and \emph{este} is already in your mouth as the pointing word for \emph{this}. The two have nothing to do with each other. The pointing \emph{este} is Latin \textbf{iste}, \emph{that one of yours}. The compass \emph{este} is Germanic, a cousin of English \textbf{east}, from a root meaning \emph{dawn}.

Two words that fell into the same shape by accident. The article tells you which is which: \textbf{el este} is a direction, plain \textbf{este} is a finger.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three points named and the fourth explained, with a warning attached.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el oeste}
  \item \emph{el norte y el oeste}
  \item \emph{el pueblo está al oeste}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What hour is \emph{oeste} named for? (The evening.) And are the compass \emph{este} and the pointing \emph{este} the same word? (No — a pure accident of shape.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el centro]{el centro — the centre, and the spike it turns on}

\label{lesson:ES-C347-centro}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{south}, then \emph{west}. (\emph{El sur}; \emph{el oeste}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la plaza — what usually sits in it.
  \item la ciudad — what has one.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{SEN-tro}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{c} before \emph{e} is soft, and \emph{tr} runs together. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el centro} — \textquotedblleft{}the centre,\textquotedblright{} and in a town, \textquotedblleft{}downtown.\textquotedblright{}

Greek \textbf{kéntron} was a \textbf{goad} — the spiked stick a farmer used to drive oxen. From the spike came the second sense: the fixed leg of a pair of compasses, the point you stick into the paper so the other leg can swing round it.

That is what a centre is. Not the middle in some vague way, but the place where the point went in.

Latin took it as \textbf{centrum} and geometry has used it ever since. English has \textbf{centre}, \textbf{central}, \textbf{concentrate} (to drive things toward one point), \textbf{eccentric} (out of centre, off the spike) and the \textbf{epicentre} of an earthquake.

In everyday Spanish, \emph{el centro} is where you go to shop and to meet people — the old middle of a town, the part built first, with the plaza and the church in it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The four points of the compass, and the still place they turn around.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el centro}
  \item \emph{el centro de la ciudad}
  \item \emph{la iglesia está en el centro}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was a \emph{kéntron} first? (A goad, a spiked stick.) And what does \textbf{eccentric} mean, word for word? (Out of the centre, off the spike.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[alrededor]{alrededor — around, and the wheel inside your knee}

\label{lesson:ES-C347-alrededor}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{west}, then \emph{the centre}. (\emph{El oeste}; \emph{el centro}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la rodilla — a little wheel, and a cousin of this.
  \item la plaza — the sort of thing you stand in the middle of.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{al-rre-de-DOR}, four beats with the weight on the last. The \emph{r} after \emph{l} is rolled, not tapped. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{alrededor} — \textquotedblleft{}around,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}round about.\textquotedblright{}

Take it apart: \textbf{al} + \textbf{rededor}. The second piece is an old Spanish word for the space surrounding a thing, and it comes from Latin \textbf{retrō}, \emph{backwards}, pulled sideways by \textbf{rota}, \emph{a wheel}.

Both ideas are in the word. Something \emph{alrededor} is behind you as well as in front, because it has gone all the way round.

\textbf{Rota} is generous. English gets \textbf{rotate}, \textbf{rotation}, \textbf{rotary}, \textbf{rotund} and \textbf{roll} from it, and Spanish gets a surprise: \textbf{la rodilla}, the knee, is Latin \textbf{rotella}, \emph{a little wheel} — the joint your leg turns on.

\textbf{Retrō} gave English \textbf{retro}, \textbf{retrograde} and \textbf{retrospect}.

So the space around you and the knee you stand on are both named for turning.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five ways to say where: north, south, west, the middle, and everything encircling it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{alrededor}
  \item \emph{alrededor de la plaza}
  \item \emph{la gente está alrededor}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does Latin \emph{rota} mean? (A wheel.) And which part of your body is a \emph{little wheel} in Spanish? (\emph{La rodilla}, the knee.)
\end{tcolorbox}
